request.lesson: A spec using the bold-identifier criteria grammar cannot cite a sibling spec's criterion by its AC-NNNN id: lint-contract-item-alignment.py rule 4 rejects every AC-NNNN token that does not resolve to the citing spec's own criteria or retired list, so a bare sibling id fails the lint. Cite sibling criteria by path plus section plus the criterion's quoted opening instead — the form the work-item-promotion-handoff spec's D4 and its plan's T2 use for the capture spec's free-text-scan criterion.

A criterion whose spec Testing Strategy declares a specific verification mode needs a plan artifact that performs exactly that check: a unit test over the same behavior does not satisfy a goal-based store-replay criterion, and the completion gate cannot close the criterion in its declared mode. The work-item-promotion-handoff plan carries a store-replay bullet beside its fixture drain so AC-0003 and AC-0004 have artifacts in the mode the spec declares for them.

A clause added to an acceptance criterion needs a stated driver in the spec's own Testing Strategy; a driver living only in the plan's mutable task list is invisible to the completion gate, so the criterion can pass while its clause is never tested. In a fourteen-round amendment review this surfaced three times — atomic publication, alien-lock refusal, and orphan-inertness clauses all landed in criteria and plan tasks but not in the gate-read scenarios until a reviewer caught each. When amending a criterion, walk every new clause into a Testing Strategy mode entry and scenario in the same commit.

When one task must assert a property of a surface another task edits, assign the edit and its pin to a single task whose Done-when names both. A split assignment — the asserting task running before the editing task's dependency order allows it — leaves a per-task gate that can never go green, and a cross-referenced parenthetical does not decide who owns the edit. The same review also caught the compressed cross-product sentence (two rules, two surfaces, one clause) that assigns both rules to both surfaces. State each rule against the one sentence it changes.
